content: The following studies and reviews explore the relationship between housing conditions, insulation, and health outcomes: 1. Austin and Russell (1997) conducted a retrospective cohort study in the Scottish Highlands to investigate the association between respiratory symptoms (such as wheeze and cough) and indoor environmental factors, including roof, cavity, and wall insulation, as well as double glazing. The study found no consistent relationship between respiratory symptoms and insulation. 2. Bray et al. (2017) analyzed the costs and health outcomes of improving population health through better social housing. This cohort study and economic analysis highlighted the potential benefits of housing improvements on health outcomes. 3. Breysse et al. (2015) examined self-reported health outcomes among elderly residents living in green-renovated public housing. The study found improvements in health outcomes associated with these renovations. 4. Grey et al. (2017) conducted a controlled before-and-after study to assess the short-term health and psychosocial impacts of domestic energy efficiency investments in low-income areas. The study demonstrated positive effects on health and well-being. 5. Homøe et al. (1999) investigated the socio-medical risk factors for acute otitis media among children in Greenland. The study did not find a significant relationship between insulation standards and episodes of acute otitis media. 6. Howden-Chapman et al. (2007) performed a cluster randomized study in New Zealand to evaluate the effects of insulating existing houses on health inequalities. The study found that insulation reduced health disparities and improved general health outcomes. 7. Iversen et al. (1986) assessed changes in health and comfort among tenants after retrofitting their housing. The study reported improvements in health and comfort following the retrofitting process. 8. Poortinga et al. (2017) conducted a multilevel analysis of a five-wave repeated cross-sectional survey to evaluate the social and health outcomes of upgrades to a national housing standard. The study found significant improvements in health and well-being. 9. Preval et al. (2017) examined the impact of improved insulation and heating on mortality risk among older individuals with prior cardiovascular or respiratory hospitalizations. The study reported a reduction in mortality risk associated with these housing improvements. 10. Tavernier et al. The study highlighted the role of housing conditions in influencing health outcomes. 11. Telfar-Barnard et al. (2011) evaluated the impact of retrofitted insulation and new heaters on health service utilization, pharmaceutical costs, and mortality in New Zealand. The study demonstrated significant health and economic benefits from these interventions. 12. Wilson et al. These studies collectively emphasize the importance of housing improvements, particularly insulation and energy efficiency, in enhancing health outcomes and reducing health disparities. However, some studies noted limitations, such as the inability to isolate the effects of insulation from other interventions or the lack of consistent findings across different health outcomes.
